rv.q: This is one of the best plays of the last 10 years, and I offer a personal guarantee that you will not be bored for a moment.
Arbery’s script, dado’s direction, and this ensemble’s haunting performance all come together for a wickedly brilliant and curious show.
But seeing it now, it seems to have missed its mark.
The production at A Red Orchid is smashingly good—tightly directed by the estimable dado with a first rate cast that has mastered this challenging, wonderfully wordy work.
It’s a sharp, compassionate play that looks honestly at Catholic conservatism, approaching it with understanding without denying its problems.
Grofsorean is extraordinary as she is steadily reduced to a stammering wreck by the mentor she idolizes.
Heroes of the Fourth Turning is a smart play that doesn’t make the mistake of thinking that debate and discourse by itself has the power to change hearts and minds.
The play itself is a challenge at two hours with no intermission, but it inspires and even forces us to consider our own societal positions.
The play is smart, intense, wide-ranging and thought-provoking, but exhausting and debilitating after a decade of violent, unnecessary and anti-intellectual conservative rhetoric.
What makes Heroes of the Fourth Turning such an unsettling production is how familiar its conversations remain after its original premiere.

cn.t: Critics largely praise this Chicago premiere as a chilling, timely mirror held up to conservative Christian America, with strong performances and sharp writing—though some find its subject matter divisive or dated.
